core: The four defining assumptions of perfect competition: many small buyers and sellers, an identical (homogeneous) product, free entry and exit, and perfect information
The firm as a price TAKER facing a horizontal (perfectly elastic) demand curve at the market price, so price = marginal revenue
The profit-maximizing output rule: produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, which in perfect competition means P = MR = MC
Short-run outcomes read off price versus average total cost: economic profit (P>ATC), break-even (P=ATC), or loss (P<ATC), with profit = (P - ATC) x Q
The shutdown idea stated briefly: a firm keeps operating in the short run only while price covers average variable cost; below minimum AVC it shuts down
Long-run entry and exit driving economic profit to zero, leaving price at the minimum of average total cost
Why long-run perfect competition is both productively efficient (output at minimum ATC) and allocatively efficient (P = MC)
supporting: Economic profit versus accounting profit: economic profit subtracts implicit (opportunity) costs, so zero economic profit still means owners cover their opportunity cost (normal profit)
Marginal revenue defined as the change in total revenue from selling one more unit
outOfScope: Monopoly, oligopoly, and monopolistic competition beyond a one-line contrast; those are price MAKERS with market power and are owned by their own topics
Derivation of the cost curves (fixed, variable, average, marginal cost) — owned by the costs topic and used here as given inputs
Deadweight loss, consumer/producer surplus welfare geometry, and market failure (externalities, public goods)
Elasticity mechanics and the full supply-and-demand shift analysis (owned by demand, supply, and market-equilibrium topics)

claims.claim: A perfectly competitive market is defined by many buyers and sellers, an identical (homogeneous) product, free entry and exit, and perfect information; it is a hypothetical benchmark rather than a literal description of most real markets.

Each firm in perfect competition is a price taker: it accepts the market price because it is too small to influence it, and if it charged even slightly more it would lose all sales to identical competitors.

Because the firm can sell any quantity at the going price, its demand curve is horizontal and its marginal revenue equals the price (P = MR); marginal revenue is the change in total revenue from selling one more unit.
The profit-maximizing firm produces the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost; in perfect competition this is the output where P = MR = MC.

At the profit-maximizing quantity, profit equals (price minus average total cost) times quantity, so the firm earns economic profit when P > ATC, breaks even when P = ATC, and takes a loss when P < ATC.
In the short run a loss-making firm keeps producing only if price at least covers average variable cost; if price falls below minimum average variable cost the firm shuts down.

Short-run economic profits attract new firms, whose entry shifts market supply right and pushes price down; sustained losses cause exit, which shifts supply left and pushes price up. This process drives economic profit toward zero, leaving price at the bottom of the average cost curve where MC crosses AC.

Economic profit subtracts both explicit costs and implicit (opportunity) costs, whereas accounting profit subtracts only explicit costs; zero economic profit therefore still means owners earn enough to cover the opportunity cost of their resources (a normal profit).
In long-run equilibrium perfect competition is productively efficient because firms produce at the minimum of average total cost (lowest possible cost per unit).

In long-run equilibrium perfect competition is allocatively efficient because firms produce where price equals marginal cost, aligning the marginal benefit buyers place on the good with its marginal cost of production.

For a firm facing market price $5 and producing where MC = 5 at q = 120 with ATC = $4.50, short-run economic profit is (5 - 4.50) x 120 = $60; once entry drives price to the minimum ATC of $4 (produced at q = 100 where MC = ATC = 4), economic profit is (4 - 4) x 100 = $0.

unsupportedExistingClaims: No prior human-written draft existed for this topic; economics is a newly initialized subject, so the lesson was authored from verified sources rather than corrected from a generated draft.
correctionsNeeded: Guarded the common conflation of zero economic profit with zero accounting profit by explicitly defining economic profit to include opportunity cost (normal profit).
Kept the shutdown rule about average VARIABLE cost distinct from the loss condition about average TOTAL cost, since these are frequently confused.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 8.1: Perfect Competition and Why It Matters
sourceRecords.notes: Primary source for the four defining assumptions (many firms with identical products, many buyers and sellers, perfect information, free entry and exit), the price-taker definition (a firm that must accept the market price and would lose all sales if it charged more), and the framing of perfect competition as a hypothetical benchmark. Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. License verified as CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for the 3e edition (consistent with other economics topics in this subject); used as reference only with original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 8.2: How Perfectly Competitive Firms Make Output Decisions
sourceRecords.notes: Supports that marginal revenue equals price for a price taker (the firm's demand curve is also its marginal revenue curve and is horizontal), the profit-maximizing rule to produce where MR = MC (hence P = MR = MC), profit computed as (Price - ATC) x Quantity, the three profit/break-even/loss cases keyed to P versus ATC, and the shutdown rule that a firm shuts down when price is below minimum average variable cost. The lesson's numeric worked example uses independently chosen and computed figures, not the book's tables. Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19; reference only, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 8.3: Entry and Exit Decisions in the Long Run
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the long-run mechanism: entry of new firms in response to economic profit shifts market supply right and lowers price; exit in response to sustained losses shifts supply left and raises price; the process drives price to the zero-profit point at the bottom of the average cost curve where marginal cost crosses average cost. Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19; reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 8.4: Efficiency in Perfectly Competitive Markets
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the two efficiency claims: productive efficiency (long-run output at the minimum of average total cost, i.e., lowest cost per unit and on the production possibility frontier) and allocative efficiency (production where price equals marginal cost, so marginal benefit equals marginal cost and the outcome is socially preferred). Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19; reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 3e, Section 7.1: Explicit and Implicit Costs, and Accounting and Economic Profit
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the economic-versus-accounting-profit distinction used to explain why 'zero economic profit' in the long run is not ruin: explicit costs are out-of-pocket payments; implicit costs are the opportunity cost of resources the firm already owns; accounting profit subtracts only explicit costs while economic profit subtracts both, so zero economic profit means owners still cover their opportunity cost (a normal profit). Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19; reference only.
